cards.front: What is weathering?
back: The breakdown of rock **in place**.

cards.front: Name the process in which pebbles collide and become smaller and rounder.
back: Attrition.

cards.front: Name the river-transport process in which large stones roll along the bed.
back: Traction.

cards.front: What is deposited on a floodplain during a flood?
back: Alluvium.

cards.front: Name the process that moves beach sediment along a coast in a zigzag.
back: Longshore drift.

cards.front: Which type of wave usually builds a beach?
back: Constructive wave.

cards.front: Give two differences between typical upland and lowland landscapes.
back: Uplands have **higher relief and steeper slopes**.
Lowlands are generally **lower and flatter**, with wider valleys.

cards.front: Explain how abrasion erodes a river channel.
back: The river carries rock fragments.
These scrape against the bed and banks, **wearing them away**.

cards.front: Explain why deposition occurs when a river enters flatter land.
back: Where a local reduction in slope causes flow to slow, the river may lose the ability to carry some of its load and deposit it.
This is not a rule that a river must get slower downstream: increasing discharge and a larger channel can raise average velocity along the whole river.

cards.front: Explain how a river cliff and slip-off slope form on a meander.
back: Faster flow erodes the outside bend, forming a **river cliff**.
Slower flow deposits sediment on the inside bend, forming a **slip-off slope**.

cards.front: Explain how geology helps create headlands and bays.
back: Softer rock is eroded rapidly to form bays.
More resistant rock erodes slowly and remains as headlands.

cards.front: Give two possible effects of building groynes.
back: They trap sediment and build a wider beach locally.
Less sediment may reach places further along the coast, increasing erosion there.

cards.front: Explain the formation of a V-shaped valley.
back: A river uses vertical erosion to cut down into its bed.
Weathering and mass movement weaken and lower the valley sides.
The river removes fallen material, leaving steep sides shaped like a V.

cards.front: Explain how a waterfall retreats to form a gorge.
back: Softer rock beneath resistant rock is eroded faster and a plunge pool forms.
The resistant overhang collapses because it is unsupported.
Repetition moves the waterfall upstream, leaving a narrow, steep-sided gorge.

cards.front: Explain how an oxbow lake forms.
back: Erosion narrows the neck of a meander.
During high flow, the river cuts through the neck and takes a straighter route.
Deposition seals the ends of the old bend, leaving an oxbow lake.

cards.front: Explain how a spit forms.
back: Longshore drift transports sediment along the coast.
Where the coastline changes direction, material continues into open water and is deposited as energy falls.
The ridge grows outward; its end may curve if wave direction changes.

cards.front: Explain how climate and geology can influence a UK river landscape.
back: Heavy or frequent rainfall raises discharge, giving a river more power to erode and transport material.
Storms can also increase flooding and floodplain deposition.
Resistant rock erodes slowly and can produce steeper features.
Softer or less resistant rock erodes more quickly, helping valleys widen.

cards.front: Explain how erosion and deposition are connected along a coast.
back: Waves erode cliffs and release sediment.
Longshore drift transports that sediment along the shoreline.
Where wave energy falls, the sediment is deposited.
This can build beaches or spits, so erosion in one place supplies landforms elsewhere.

cards.front: Explain how natural processes and people combine to shape the River Wye landscape.
back: The Wye rises on Plynlimon, where high rainfall and steep slopes produce rapid runoff and energetic erosion.
Downstream, tributaries raise discharge and gentler relief allows meanders, floodplains and deposition.
Carboniferous Limestone creates a steep lower gorge around Symonds Yat, showing that geology modifies the usual downstream pattern.
Farming and building alter runoff, while natural flood-management work with more than 140 landowners slows and stores water upstream.

cards.front: Explain why managing one part of the North Norfolk coast can affect another part.
back: Eroding cliffs supply sediment, and longshore drift moves it along particular coastal frontages. Defences such as groynes retain material locally and may reduce supply farther along that route.
Blakeney Point grows through westward transport along its frontage, while sediment at Happisburgh generally moves south. These are not one simple Happisburgh-to-Blakeney route.
A narrower beach farther along a local transport route can expose land to more wave energy, so management needs to consider effects beyond the defended site.

cards.front: What is the difference between relief and geology?
back: Relief is the height and shape of the land. Geology concerns its rocks and their structure.

cards.front: Why is it incorrect to call every sedimentary rock soft?
back: Resistance depends on the particular rock, its cementation, cracks and layers. Limestone can form steep resistant landscapes even though it is sedimentary.

cards.front: Does a glaciated landscape have to be separate from an upland landscape?
back: No. Glaciated describes the effect of former ice, while upland describes relief. The same place can be both.

cards.front: Why does freeze–thaw weathering require repeated temperature changes?
back: Water freezes and expands in cracks, then thaws so water can enter again. Repeated cycles widen the cracks; continuous freezing alone is not repeated freeze–thaw.

cards.front: How does chemical weathering affect limestone?
back: Weakly acidic water reacts with and dissolves calcium carbonate, gradually changing and removing the rock.

cards.front: How does sliding differ from rotational slumping?
back: Sliding follows a relatively flat failure surface. Slumping rotates along a curved surface and can leave stepped or tilted material.

cards.front: Why is attrition different from abrasion?
back: Attrition changes carried particles as they collide with each other. Abrasion wears the bed, banks or cliff as carried material scrapes or strikes it.

cards.front: What separates suspension from transport in solution?
back: Suspension carries fine solid particles within water. Solution carries dissolved minerals.

cards.front: What is a drainage-basin watershed?
back: The boundary separating land draining to one river system from land draining to another. It often follows high ground.

cards.front: What happens at a confluence?
back: A tributary joins another river, generally adding water and increasing its discharge below the junction.

cards.front: Why can average river velocity increase downstream despite a gentler gradient?
back: Tributaries add discharge and the channel becomes wider and deeper. Less of the flowing water is affected by friction relative to its volume, making the channel more efficient.

cards.front: Does every gorge have to form by waterfall retreat?
back: No. Retreat can form a gorge, but river incision into resistant rock can also produce a steep valley, as illustrated by the lower Wye.

cards.front: Why is coarser alluvium often deposited beside the channel during a flood?
back: Water slows sharply as it leaves the channel. Coarser particles settle first, while finer particles travel farther across the floodplain.

cards.front: What is fetch, and how can it affect waves?
back: Fetch is the distance of open water over which wind blows. A longer fetch can allow larger waves to develop when other conditions support it.

cards.front: Why can a bay favour deposition while its headlands experience erosion?
back: Wave refraction concentrates energy on projecting headlands, while the bay is relatively sheltered, allowing sediment to settle.

cards.front: Why can salt marsh develop behind a spit?
back: The spit shelters the water, allowing fine sediment to settle. Salt-tolerant vegetation traps additional sediment and helps the marsh build.

cards.front: Why should Happisburgh not be described as the direct sediment source for Blakeney Point?
back: Transport directions differ along these frontages. Drift at Happisburgh is generally southward, while the Blakeney frontage has westward transport.

cards.front: Which named North Norfolk place illustrates wind deposition and vegetation trapping sand?
back: Holkham. Wind moves dry sand inland, and plants such as marram grass trap it and bind the dunes.
